title: Reverse Engineering with Karnaugh Maps
excerpt: A hands-on, complete introduction to Karnaugh maps, built around a hidden three-input circuit you help reverse-engineer.

body.text: What's Actually Inside the Black Box?

content.text: Picture a sealed black box with three switches on the front and a single light on the back. Flip the switches, the light goes on or off. You have no idea what's wired up inside. That's the whole premise of this post, and it's also the honest starting point for a lot of digital logic design.
Below is the box. Flip A, B, and C in any order. Every new combination you try gets logged in the table beside it. Try to fill in all eight rows before you keep reading.

body.text: From a Table to a Formula

content.text: Once all eight rows are filled in, you technically know everything about this circuit. Give it any input, and you can look up the output. But a lookup table isn't a formula, and a formula is what lets you build the circuit out of real gates, reason about it, or shrink it down to fewer parts.

You could grind through this with Boolean algebra: write the sum of the minterms where the output is 1, then apply the distributive law, absorption, De Morgan's theorem, and hope you land somewhere simple. It works. It's also slow and easy to mess up by hand, especially past three variables.
Karnaugh maps exist so you don't have to do that grinding. A K-map takes the same truth table and rearranges it into a grid where the pattern practically draws itself.
Only a few rules govern a legal K-map group:
• A group's size has to be a power of two: 1, 2, 4, 8, and so on.
• Groups must be rectangular, including wraparound at the edges of the map, since the far column is adjacent to the first one under Gray code.
• Bigger is better. A group of four cancels out two variables instead of one, so look for the largest legal group before settling for something smaller.
• Groups are allowed to overlap. The same 1 can belong to more than one group if that's what it takes to cover every 1 with the fewest, largest groups.

→ Once every 1 in the map belongs to at least one group, each combination has been accounted for. OR the terms from each group together, and that sum is your simplified function! You can now build a circuit out of gates, reason about it, or shrink it down to fewer parts.

When a '1' in a Karnaugh map can only be covered by a single group, that group is called an essential prime implicant and must be included in your final expression. For the remaining '1's that can be covered by multiple groups, always select the combination that minimizes both the total number of groups and their sizes.
If you found A'C and AB in the map above, you already know the box's real function: F = A'C + AB. Three switches and a light bulb, reduced to two terms.

The move from truth table to gate-level formula is the whole game of digital logic. Everything else (adders, multiplexers, memory, whole processors) is the same trick, applied over and over at bigger scale.
